planner.summary: The contract works if the current client keeps its two days and the new work is scoped to fixed deliverables rather than open-ended support.
assumptions: The current client keeps needing two days a week.
One part-time assistant can cover the routine part of the new contract.
The contract has a fixed scope rather than unlimited revisions.

options.title: Take the contract with a capped scope
options.description: Sign for six months, name the deliverables, and keep the current client at two days.

options.title: Take a three-month trial
options.description: Ask for a shorter initial term so the arrangement can be reviewed before hiring.

evidence.text: The person has three months of savings, which covers a short ramp-up.
A supplied rate card lists day rates for this kind of work.

counterarguments: A capped scope may be unacceptable to the client.
Hiring before the first invoice arrives puts the savings buffer at risk.
disagreements: Whether to hire before or after the first contract payment.
missing_info: The contract's payment terms and notice period.
How much of the new work the assistant can actually take on.

experiment.title: Run one paid trial deliverable
steps: Agree one small paid deliverable with the client.
Record how many hours it actually took.
experiment.success_signal: The deliverable is paid on time and takes less than the estimate.
experiment.stop_signal: It takes more than twice the estimated hours or the client delays payment.

questions: Can you ask for a three-month initial term without losing the offer?
What would you need to see before offering someone a job?

critic.summary: The plan fails if the current client's two days expand, if the contract's scope is open-ended, or if hiring happens before the first payment lands.
assumptions: The current client's workload stays at two days a week.
The assistant can be found and trained within a month.

options.title: Delay hiring until the first invoice is paid
options.description: Take the contract alone, then hire once cash has arrived.

evidence.text: The person named three months of savings as the available resource.

counterarguments: Delaying the hire may mean missing the contract's first deadline.
The savings buffer may not cover both a slow month and a hiring cost.
disagreements: Whether the savings buffer is large enough to hire before payment.
missing_info: The total cost of hiring, including any equipment.
Whether the current client has already signalled a change in hours.

experiment.title: Two-week solo stress test
steps: Do the new work alone for two weeks while keeping the current client.
Log every hour against the plan.
Compare the log with the contract's deadline.
experiment.success_signal: The work fits inside the hours you actually have.
experiment.stop_signal: You are more than a day behind within the first two weeks.

questions: What is the first sign that the current client wants more than two days?
How many weeks of savings are you willing to spend on the ramp-up?

research.summary: Most of the plan rests on the person's own context. The contract terms, the assistant's cost and the client's renewal are all unsupported by anything supplied.
assumptions: The supplied rate card is relevant to this kind of contract.
The person's savings figure is current.

options.title: Gather the four missing facts before signing
options.description: Treat the contract as provisional until terms, costs and renewal are written down.

evidence.text: The rate card is the only supplied source and covers day rates, not contract terms.
Nothing supplied describes the contract's payment schedule.

counterarguments: Waiting for perfect information may lose the offer.
The rate card may be out of date.
disagreements: How much missing information is enough to decide.
missing_info: Written payment terms and notice period.
The real all-in cost of a part-time assistant.
Whether the current client has renewed for next year.

experiment.title: Ask for the terms in writing
steps: Request the contract's payment schedule and notice period in writing.
Ask two people who have hired part-time help what it cost.
Write down the answers next to the plan.
experiment.success_signal: The terms and costs are written down and fit the savings buffer.
experiment.stop_signal: The client will not put terms in writing.

questions: Which single missing fact would change your decision most?
Who could confirm the real cost of part-time help?

human_impact.summary: The arrangement affects the current client, a future assistant and the people sharing the person's time. The assistant carries the most risk if the contract ends early.
assumptions: The assistant would depend on these hours for income.
The current client would notice reduced availability.

options.title: Hire with a clear trial period
options.description: Offer a short, explicit trial so the assistant is not exposed to an open-ended commitment.

options.title: Stay solo and reduce the contract scope
options.description: Protect the current client's time and avoid taking on someone else's income risk.

evidence.text: The person listed time with family among their priorities.

counterarguments: A trial period can still feel insecure to the person hired.
Staying solo may mean turning down work the person wants.
disagreements: Whether it is fair to hire someone before the contract is secure.
missing_info: Whether the assistant would have other income.
How the current client would be told about reduced availability.

experiment.title: Talk to one potential assistant before deciding
steps: Describe the six-month scope and the trial period honestly.
Ask what security they would need.
Write down their answer before making an offer.
experiment.success_signal: The expectations on both sides are explicit and written down.
experiment.stop_signal: You would need to hide the contract's uncertainty to make the offer.

questions: Who carries the cost if the contract ends in month two?
Which relationship are you least willing to strain?

synthesizer.summary: The real choice is not contract versus no contract. It is how much risk to place on the assistant and the savings buffer before the first payment arrives.
assumptions: The contract is real but its terms are not yet written down.
The current client's two days are not negotiable in the short term.

options.title: Contract first, hire after payment
options.description: Accept the scope, deliver the first milestone alone, then hire with clearer cash.

options.title: Contract with a trial hire
options.description: Hire on an explicit short trial with hours that the savings buffer can cover.

options.title: Decline and protect the current work
options.description: Keep the two days and revisit when the current client renews.

evidence.text: The rate card is the only supplied source and does not cover contract terms.
The payment schedule is unknown, which is the largest unresolved fact.

counterarguments: Waiting for payment may cost the contract.
A trial hire may not be enough capacity for the first deadline.
disagreements: The planner and critic disagree on whether to hire before the first payment.
The human-impact reviewer would accept a trial; the critic treats any early hire as the main risk.
questions: Which risk can you actually afford: a delayed payment or a delayed hire?
What would make you reject all three options?
tradeoffs: Cash safety versus delivery capacity in the first month.
The assistant's security versus your savings buffer.
Keeping the current client's trust versus taking the larger contract.
synthesizer.recommendation: Ask for written terms and take the contract, but delay the hire until the first payment arrives or the scope is confirmed in writing.
